h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in San Antonio
intro: San Antonio is one of the few big Texas cities where the historic preservation office is as important to a rehab budget as the foundation contractor. A large share of the close-in housing that investors want, from King William and Dignowity Hill to Monte Vista and Government Hill, sits inside designated historic districts with exterior design review. Beyond those districts you find small pier-and-beam houses on the Westside and South Side that have been added onto over generations, and miles of postwar and 1970s ranches on the north and northeast sides that need systems, roofs and kitchens. Genstone Construction coordinates vetted, licensed contractors across San Antonio for investors, lenders and servicers, managed by our estimators and field managers from headquarters in Romeoville, Illinois. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and refines your ARV before you commit, and every job runs on a detailed scope, a draw schedule tied to completed work and a single field manager.
housingStock:
San Antonio's housing history is layered in a way few Texas cities can match. The oldest investor-relevant stock sits just south and east of downtown. King William and Lavaca have nineteenth-century limestone and frame houses built by German merchants and craftsmen, alongside Victorian cottages. Dignowity Hill and Government Hill on the East Side have folk Victorian and early twentieth-century frame houses, many in rough condition. These are expensive houses to restore correctly, with lime-based mortar, old-growth wood siding, tall windows and porches that the historic office expects to see repaired rather than replaced.

Moving north, Tobin Hill, Beacon Hill, Monte Vista, Alta Vista and Woodlawn Lake were built out from the 1910s through the 1930s with Craftsman bungalows, Tudor and Spanish eclectic cottages and, in Monte Vista, large period homes. Nearly all sit on pier-and-beam foundations. The Westside and South Side, including Prospect Hill, Las Palmas, Harlandale and Highland Park, are dominated by small frame houses from the 1920s through the 1950s, often expanded with rear rooms, enclosed porches and garage conversions built over decades, sometimes without permits.

After the war, the city spread north and northeast with slab-on-grade brick and frame ranches in neighborhoods around Northwood, Oak Park, Windcrest and the areas near the military bases. The 1970s and 1980s added tract subdivisions farther out along Loop 410 and Loop 1604. Those homes bring their own era's issues: aluminum wiring in some, polybutylene supply lines in some later builds, original HVAC duct systems and roofs that have been through more than one major hailstorm. Across the city, the biggest swing factor is the ground. East and south sides sit on expansive clay that moves with rain and drought, while the north side sits on shallow limestone and caliche, which is more stable but harder to dig for plumbing repairs.

commonIssues.title: Historic district design review
commonIssues.body: A large number of San Antonio's older neighborhoods are local historic districts, and the Office of Historic Preservation and the Historic and Design Review Commission review exterior changes there. Replacing wood windows, swapping siding, changing porch details, adding square footage or building a new fence can all require a Certificate of Appropriateness. Investors who skip this step can be ordered to undo work. We check district status before scoping so the exterior plan is one the city will approve.

commonIssues.title: Pier-and-beam leveling on clay
commonIssues.body: Older homes on the East Side, Westside and South Side usually sit on pier-and-beam foundations, sometimes on wood blocks or short concrete piers that have settled unevenly in the clay. Floors slope, doors bind and interior walls crack. Leveling, adding piers and replacing rotted sills and joists is a routine but important part of most scopes. We sequence that work first so new drywall, tile and trim are not cracked by later adjustments.

commonIssues.title: Unpermitted additions and conversions
commonIssues.body: Many Westside and South Side houses have grown over time with back rooms, enclosed porches, converted garages and add-on bathrooms. Some were built well, others were not, and many were never permitted. Appraisers may not count unpermitted square footage, and lenders may ask for it to be legalized or removed. We evaluate each addition's framing, electrical and plumbing and price the options so you can decide how to handle it before closing.

commonIssues.title: Hail and storm roof damage
commonIssues.body: San Antonio sits in a region that sees damaging spring hail, and the April 2016 storm that hit the north and northwest sides led to roof replacements across large parts of those neighborhoods. Many roofs have been replaced since, but some houses carry older patches or hidden damage. We inspect shingles, flashing, vents and decking and look at the age of the roof, then price repair or replacement so the buyer's inspector and insurer have nothing to flag.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint, asbestos and old wiring
commonIssues.body: Most of the older stock predates 1978, so lead-based paint is common on siding, trim and windows, and renovation must follow lead-safe practices. Postwar homes may contain asbestos in floor tile, mastic, ceiling texture or siding. Prewar homes often have remnants of knob-and-tube or cloth-sheathed wiring mixed with later circuits. We budget for testing and for rewiring where needed, so the renovation is safe and passes electrical inspection through the city.

investorMarket:
San Antonio's investor map follows the city's history and its military and medical employers.

Close-in historic neighborhoods such as King William, Southtown, Lavaca, Tobin Hill, Monte Vista and Beacon Hill support retail flips and higher-end rentals, but only for investors comfortable with historic district review and restoration-level budgets. Buyers there pay for authentic detail, and cutting corners on the exterior can backfire with both the city and the market. Dignowity Hill and Government Hill on the East Side have seen steady reinvestment and suit investors willing to take on larger restoration projects.

The Westside and South Side, including Prospect Hill, Harlandale, Highland Park and Palm Heights, are dominated by buy-and-hold and BRRRR investors. Houses are small and purchase prices are generally lower, but scopes often include foundation leveling, electrical updates, plumbing and decisions about unpermitted additions. Rental demand is steady from local families and workers across the city.

Northeast and north-central neighborhoods near Joint Base San Antonio–Fort Sam Houston and Randolph, and the west side near Lackland, offer brick ranches that rent well to military households and civilian employees. These areas fit BRRRR and long-term rental strategies and are often simpler to renovate than the older core. Farther north along Loop 1604, newer tract homes trade more like suburban product, and investor activity there focuses on rental turns rather than heavy rehab.
permits:
Residential permits in San Antonio are issued by the City of San Antonio Development Services Department. Foundation repair, structural changes, new or altered plumbing and electrical, HVAC replacement, re-roofing, window replacement in many cases, and additions require permits and inspections. Licensed plumbers, electricians and air conditioning contractors, licensed through the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners or the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, must pull the trade permits.

San Antonio's historic preservation program is one of the most active in Texas. The Office of Historic Preservation and the Historic and Design Review Commission review exterior work on properties in local historic districts and on individual landmarks, and some work can be approved administratively while larger changes go to the commission. Unpermitted or unapproved exterior work in a district can lead to stop-work orders and required corrections. On the far north side, properties over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone are subject to additional rules for impervious cover and water quality, which can affect additions or new paving. Addresses outside city limits, including suburban cities and unincorporated Bexar County, follow their own permitting offices. We confirm jurisdiction and district status for every property before scoping.
climate:
San Antonio's climate is hot and somewhat drier than the Gulf Coast, but it brings its own risks. Long summers stress air conditioning systems and dry out clay soils, which accelerates foundation movement on the east and south sides. Exterior painting, roofing and concrete work are scheduled for early mornings during the hottest months.

Spring brings hail and severe thunderstorms, and the region sits in what is often called Flash Flood Alley, where heavy rain can turn creeks and low-water crossings dangerous quickly. Houses near creeks and in low areas may have flood history worth checking. Winters are usually mild, but hard freezes like Winter Storm Uri in 2021 burst pipes across the city, especially in older pier-and-beam homes with exposed plumbing underneath. We include freeze protection and pipe insulation in scopes for crawlspace houses.

faqs.q: Do you work in suburbs like Converse, Schertz and Alamo Heights?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate licensed contractors across Bexar County and the surrounding area, including Converse, Live Oak, Universal City, Schertz, Leon Valley, Helotes, New Braunfels and the incorporated cities of Alamo Heights and Olmos Park. Each has its own building department and inspection process. We confirm jurisdiction for each address before scoping so the permit plan reflects the right city rather than assuming San Antonio rules apply.

faqs.q: How do historic district rules affect my San Antonio rehab?
faqs.a: In a local historic district, exterior changes like window replacement, siding, porch work, roofing materials, fences and additions may require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Office of Historic Preservation or the Historic and Design Review Commission. Interior work is generally not reviewed. We check status during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and design the exterior scope to meet the guidelines, which often means repairing original wood windows and siding rather than replacing them.

faqs.q: Should I buy a Westside house with unpermitted additions?
faqs.a: It can work, but you need to know what you are buying. Some additions are sound and can be permitted after inspection with modest corrections. Others have undersized framing, unsafe wiring or poor drainage and are better removed. Appraisers may not count unpermitted space, which affects your ARV. We evaluate each addition and price both options so the decision is part of your offer, not a surprise after closing.

faqs.q: Do I pay anything upfront?
faqs.a: No. Genstone does not take upfront payment. Construction draws are tied to completed work you can verify through photos and milestone documentation, and final payment comes after completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris costs are included in every estimate. Our work carries a one-year workmanship warranty that excludes tenant damage and normal wear, and our billing team manages lien waivers and contractor compliance so your records are clean for your lender or buyer.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in San Antonio, TX | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: San Antonio flips scoped for Tobin Hill, Beacon Hill and northeast ranch buyers: historic review, pier leveling, hail roofs and draws tied to completed work.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in San Antonio
fix-flip.intro: Flipping in San Antonio splits into two very different businesses. Inside the historic core, in Tobin Hill, Beacon Hill, Monte Vista, Lavaca and Dignowity Hill, you are selling a restored early twentieth-century home to a buyer who wants original character, and you are doing it under the eye of the Office of Historic Preservation. Outside the core, in the brick ranch neighborhoods of the northeast and north-central city, you are selling a clean, updated house against other updated ranches, and speed and systems matter more than period detail. Genstone scopes flips for both. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repair costs, checks district status and refines your ARV before you commit capital, and our field manager coordinates licensed San Antonio contractors through permits, approvals and finish work.

sections.h2: Restoration flips inside the historic districts
sections.body:
A Craftsman bungalow in Beacon Hill or a Victorian cottage in Dignowity Hill can be a strong flip, but the exterior budget looks different than it would elsewhere. In a local historic district, the city generally expects original wood windows, siding, porch columns and trim to be repaired rather than replaced, and changes visible from the street need approval. Planning for that from the start keeps the project on schedule.

Inside, buyers in these neighborhoods want the house to feel original and work like new. That usually means refinishing original pine or oak floors, keeping or recreating period trim and doors, rewiring to remove old knob-and-tube or cloth-sheathed circuits, replacing galvanized and cast-iron plumbing, adding central air with ductwork routed carefully through attic and crawlspace, and building a kitchen and baths that suit the house. Leveling the pier-and-beam foundation comes first. We price multiple finish levels so you can match the comps on your block rather than overbuilding for the neighborhood.

sections.h2: Ranch flips on the northeast and north sides
sections.body:
The postwar and 1970s ranches near Fort Sam Houston, Randolph, Northwood and along Loop 410 are a different kind of flip. Buyers here include military households, medical workers and first-time buyers using FHA or VA financing, and their inspectors will focus on the roof, foundation, HVAC and electrical. A flip that looks great but has a hail-damaged roof or an undersized AC system will get renegotiated.

We scope these houses with the inspection report in mind. Roofs are checked for hail damage and age. Slabs are evaluated for movement, especially on clay soils east of downtown. Electrical panels are upgraded where needed, and aluminum branch wiring is addressed if present. HVAC is sized correctly and ductwork sealed. Then we focus visible spend on what buyers in these areas value: open kitchen layouts, updated baths, durable flooring and good curb appeal. VA and FHA appraisals also look for safety and condition items like handrails, working windows and smoke alarms, which we include in the punch list.

sections.h2: Timeline, permits and carrying costs in San Antonio
sections.body:
Carrying costs are where flips lose money, and in San Antonio the biggest variable is often approval time rather than construction time. Historic district projects may need a Certificate of Appropriateness before exterior work starts, and some items go to the Historic and Design Review Commission rather than being approved by staff. We submit early and sequence interior work so crews keep moving while exterior approvals are pending.

Permits for foundation, plumbing, electrical, HVAC and roofing go through the City of San Antonio Development Services Department, and inspections must pass in order. Our field manager stacks inspections and coordinates trades so the house does not sit idle between them. Weather also matters: spring storms can delay roofing, and summer heat slows exterior work. Because Genstone ties draws to completed work and documents progress with milestone photos, you can track the schedule without visiting the site, and the documentation helps when you share updates with lenders or partners.

faqs.q: Can I replace windows on a historic San Antonio flip?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but expect scrutiny. In local historic districts the city generally prefers repair of original wood windows, and replacement usually requires approval and a product that matches the original design. Rear or non-visible windows may be treated differently. We assess window condition, check district guidelines and price restoration and approved replacement options so you can compare cost against the schedule and the sale price.

faqs.q: How do VA buyers affect a San Antonio flip?
faqs.a: With several military installations in the area, VA financing is common. VA appraisals check minimum property requirements, including safe electrical, working heat and cooling, sound roofs and no peeling paint on older homes. Building those items into the scope avoids repair requests after the appraisal. We review the punch list with VA and FHA requirements in mind so the house is ready for those buyers.

faqs.q: What does a typical San Antonio flip scope include?
faqs.a: It depends on the house. A historic bungalow usually needs foundation leveling, rewiring, new plumbing, central air, a kitchen, baths and exterior restoration. A northeast ranch usually needs roof work, HVAC, electrical updates, a kitchen, baths, flooring and paint. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review produces a line-item scope with multiple finish levels so you can see the options before you buy.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in San Antonio, TX | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in San Antonio near Lackland, Fort Sam and the Westside: rental-grade finishes, permitted additions and systems that hold up at the refi appraisal.
brrrr.intro: San Antonio's rental demand is anchored by Joint Base San Antonio, the South Texas Medical Center, a large health care and services workforce and steady local household formation, which makes it a natural BRRRR market. The best candidates tend to be brick ranches on the northeast and west sides near the bases and small frame houses on the Westside and South Side that need a complete systems update. In both cases, the rehab has to satisfy an appraiser on the refinance and then hold up to tenants for years. Genstone scopes BRRRR projects with both in mind. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and ARV before you buy, and Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans if you want to plan the refinance alongside the work. One field manager coordinates licensed local contractors and permits throughout.

sections.body:
San Antonio appraisers compare your property to recent nearby sales and adjust for condition and usable square footage. That second part matters a lot on the Westside and South Side, where many houses have additions that were never permitted. If a back bedroom or converted garage is not legal, the appraiser may not count it, and your ARV drops. We evaluate each addition, then price the options of permitting it after corrections or removing it, so your BRRRR math reflects what the appraiser will actually see.

The other big appraisal drivers are systems and visible condition. A house with a new roof, leveled foundation, updated electrical, modern plumbing and reliable HVAC appraises better than one with nice finishes over old systems. We target finishes at the level comparable rentals and sales support, typically durable vinyl plank, mid-range counters and updated fixtures, and spend the rest on the items an appraiser and underwriter will check. Permit records and foundation documentation are organized so you can answer questions quickly.

A San Antonio rental needs to handle long cooling seasons, occasional hard freezes and tenants who move every few years. We design for that. HVAC is sized correctly, ductwork is sealed and attic insulation is improved where thin, which keeps cooling bills manageable and reduces service calls. On pier-and-beam houses, exposed plumbing under the floor is insulated and protected after the lesson of Winter Storm Uri, when many older homes lost supply lines in the crawlspace.

Inside, we use waterproof vinyl plank, semi-gloss paint in wet areas, solid cabinets and standard fixtures that are easy to replace. Exterior work focuses on roofs, gutters and drainage that keeps water away from the foundation, especially on clay soils east and south of downtown. On older frame houses, we repair or replace rotted siding and trim and use paint systems that hold up to the sun. These choices keep turnover costs down and protect the value you need for the next refinance.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods that suit BRRRR in San Antonio
sections.body:
Brick ranches on the northeast side near Fort Sam Houston and Randolph and on the west side near Lackland are a common BRRRR fit because they rent well to military and civilian households and tend to have simpler scopes than the older core. Westside and South Side frame houses in Prospect Hill, Harlandale, Highland Park and Palm Heights can work well too, with lower purchase prices but more extensive scopes that often include leveling, rewiring, re-plumbing and decisions about additions.

We are more cautious with houses in historic districts for BRRRR, because restoration-level exterior requirements raise costs without always raising rents. We also check flood exposure on properties near creeks and in low-lying areas. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, we assess all of this and give you a realistic scope and ARV so you can see whether the refinance works before you buy. If a house only pencils as a flip, or not at all, we would rather tell you that than help you hold a property that cannot pull its capital back out.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial refinance my San Antonio BRRRR?
faqs.a: It can. Within the Genstone Companies, Genstone Financial writes DSCR rental loans alongside fix-and-flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. A DSCR loan qualifies based on the property's rental income, which suits many BRRRR investors with several San Antonio rentals. Using Genstone Financial is optional. We provide the same line-item scope, draw records, permit sign-offs and completion photos to any lender you choose, so your refinance package is ready when the appraisal is ordered.

faqs.q: Should I permit an unpermitted addition before refinancing?
faqs.a: Often, yes, if the addition is sound. Legal square footage typically counts in the appraisal, while unpermitted space may not. Permitting may require corrections to framing, electrical or plumbing to meet code. If the addition is poorly built, removing it can be the better choice. We price both paths so you can see which one produces the stronger refinance and the cleaner rental.

faqs.q: Do military tenants affect how I renovate?
faqs.a: Military households often relocate on predictable cycles, and many use base housing offices or relocation services that expect clean, safe, well-maintained homes. Durable finishes, reliable HVAC, good security and a clean exterior help these homes lease quickly. Proximity to Lackland, Fort Sam Houston or Randolph also matters more than finish level, so we keep the spend practical and put it into the systems that generate calls.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in San Antonio, TX | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: San Antonio single-family rental rehabs: Westside pier-and-beam houses, base-area brick ranches and north-side tract homes held to one portfolio standard.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovations in San Antonio
rental-renovation.intro: A San Antonio rental portfolio often mixes three very different houses: a 1940s frame cottage on the Westside sitting on wood blocks, a 1960s brick ranch a few miles from Fort Sam Houston, and a 1990s tract home off Loop 1604. Each fails differently, and a single generic rehab spec will overspend on one and underspend on another. Genstone works with landlords, funds and institutional owners to renovate and turn single-family rentals across San Antonio and its suburbs. We start from one written portfolio standard, then adjust for each era of house, coordinate licensed local contractors and assign one field manager per property. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps acquisitions teams price houses before they buy, and our scopes and draw records give asset managers a clear view of spending.

sections.h2: Adjusting the standard to San Antonio house types
sections.body:
Our rental standard sets the baseline for every property: waterproof vinyl plank, one paint family, stock cabinet sizes, standard fixtures, sealed ductwork and correctly sized HVAC, plus the safety items every rental needs. Where San Antonio requires judgment is in how that baseline applies to each kind of house.

On Westside and South Side frame houses, the standard expands underneath and inside the walls. Floors are leveled, rotted sills and joists replaced, supply lines in the crawlspace insulated against freezes, and old cloth-sheathed circuits removed. Additions get a hard look for framing, roof tie-ins and wiring. On northeast and west-side brick ranches, the attention shifts to roofs that have been through hail, slab movement on clay soils, drain lines under the slab and original electrical panels. On north-side tract homes from the 1980s and 1990s, the work is usually lighter, but we check for polybutylene supply lines in some builds, aging water heaters in garages and attics, and HVAC equipment near the end of its life. Applying the standard with those differences in mind keeps per-unit costs predictable without ignoring the problems specific to each house.

sections.h2: Covering the portfolio across Bexar County
sections.body:
San Antonio rental portfolios often extend beyond city limits into Converse, Live Oak, Universal City, Schertz, Kirby and unincorporated Bexar County, where much of the newer tract housing sits. Each of those areas has its own building department and inspection practices, and some suburban subdivisions have homeowners associations with their own exterior rules. A portfolio program has to respect those differences while keeping quality, pricing and reporting consistent.

Genstone uses one written standard and one reporting format across all of them, while our licensed, insured contractor network performs the work locally. Each property gets a field manager who handles permits, inspections, lien waivers and contractor compliance in the correct jurisdiction. Progress, photos and draw requests are available without site visits. Our estimators also flag properties that need capital work beyond a turn, such as foundation leveling on a Westside cottage or a roof replacement on a ranch that took hail, so annual budgets reflect actual conditions rather than averages. When a house sits inside a historic district, we note any exterior items that would require review before work begins.

The best turns in San Antonio are timed to the weather. A vacancy in early spring is the right window to service or replace HVAC equipment before summer demand ties up every contractor in the city. A vacancy after the spring storm season is a good time to inspect roofs and gutters for hail and wind damage. A fall turn on a pier-and-beam house is the moment to check crawlspace plumbing insulation and skirting before the first hard freeze.

We scope turns to catch these predictable failures, not just repaint and clean. That means testing smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, rekeying locks, clearing AC condensate lines, checking water heater age and pressure relief valves, resealing tubs and showers and looking for new cracks that indicate foundation movement. Genstone Field Services also handles occupied maintenance, inspections and code compliance, so one organization can support both the renovation and the ongoing upkeep. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work we perform and excludes tenant damage and normal wear.

faqs.q: Do you renovate rentals near the military bases?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our San Antonio rental projects are brick ranches on the northeast side near Fort Sam Houston and Randolph and on the west side near Lackland. These homes rent to military and civilian households who expect clean, safe, well-maintained properties. We focus on reliable HVAC, sound roofs, secure doors and windows and durable finishes so the homes lease quickly and hold up through frequent moves.

faqs.q: Can you handle pier-and-beam rentals on the Westside?
faqs.a: Yes. Pier-and-beam homes are common on the Westside and South Side, and we coordinate licensed foundation contractors to level floors, add or replace piers and repair framing. We also insulate exposed plumbing in the crawlspace and improve skirting so pipes are better protected in freezes. Doing that work during a vacancy is far easier than scheduling it around a tenant.

faqs.q: How do you keep costs consistent across many properties?
faqs.a: We work from a written finish and systems standard that you approve, which covers flooring, paint, fixtures, cabinets and HVAC specifications. Estimates use the same line-item format for every property, so you can compare houses and track spending easily. We adjust only where a property's age or condition requires it, and we explain each adjustment in the scope, such as extra crawlspace work on a Westside cottage.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & Fourplex Renovation in San Antonio, TX | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: San Antonio 2–4 unit renovations: Tobin Hill and Five Points duplexes, Monte Vista conversions and base-area fourplexes, phased around tenants and permits.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Small Multifamily Renovations in San Antonio
multifamily-renovation.intro: San Antonio's small multifamily buildings are concentrated in a few distinct places. Tobin Hill, Five Points and the streets around San Antonio College hold frame duplexes and early twentieth-century houses that were split into apartments decades ago. Monte Vista and Alta Vista have large period homes converted into several units. The near Westside has houses with a casita or second dwelling behind the main structure. And the northeast side near Fort Sam Houston has brick duplexes and fourplexes from the 1960s and 1970s built for military and civilian renters. Each type has different shared systems, code questions and approval paths. Genstone helps investors renovate 2–4 unit buildings across San Antonio by coordinating licensed local contractors, phasing work around tenants and managing permits and historic approvals. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the property before you buy.

sections.h2: Converted houses in Tobin Hill, Five Points and Monte Vista
sections.body:
Many of San Antonio's older multifamily properties started life as single-family homes. Over the decades, owners divided them into two, three or four units, often adding kitchens and baths in former bedrooms and running new wiring and plumbing through existing walls. The results vary widely. Some conversions are well documented and well built. Others have shared electrical circuits between units, drain lines that run long distances with poor slope, and little fire separation between apartments.

These buildings usually sit on pier-and-beam foundations that need leveling, and many are in or near historic districts where exterior changes require review. Our scope starts with a careful inventory of each unit's electrical, plumbing and HVAC, then identifies shared systems and safety gaps. Typical work includes upgrading the electrical service and separating circuits, replacing galvanized and cast-iron plumbing, improving separation and smoke detection between units and adding or upgrading HVAC that suits the layout. We also look at whether the number of units is a legal use under current zoning, which affects both financing and long-term plans.

On the northeast side near Fort Sam Houston and along the corridors toward Randolph, small brick duplexes and fourplexes from the 1960s and 1970s rent steadily to military households, medical workers and students. These buildings are simpler than the old converted houses, but they have their own issues. Slabs on clay soils move, cracking brick and drywall. Original windows are often single-pane aluminum. HVAC systems may be through-wall units or aging split systems added piecemeal. Roofs may have hail damage, and shared drain lines under the slab can be cast iron nearing the end of its life.

We scope these buildings for durability and efficiency: foundation evaluation and repair where needed, roof replacement when warranted, insulated windows, properly sized HVAC for each unit, plumbing updates and durable interiors that can be turned quickly. Because these buildings often have tenants in place, we phase work unit by unit and schedule shared-system work with notice. Genstone Field Services can handle occupied maintenance in units not yet renovated, keeping the building in good condition throughout.

San Antonio uses a Unified Development Code with zoning districts that determine how many units a lot can hold. Many older converted houses and small apartment buildings predate current zoning and exist as nonconforming uses. That status generally allows continued use, but it can limit expansion and affect rebuilding after significant damage. Confirming zoning and the legal number of units before you buy is important, especially when financing depends on unit count.

Renovation permits go through the City of San Antonio Development Services Department. Properties in local historic districts, including much of Tobin Hill, Monte Vista and the near East Side, need Office of Historic Preservation or Historic and Design Review Commission approval for exterior changes like window replacement, porch work, new stairs or additions. Multi-unit buildings are also subject to fire and life-safety requirements for separation, egress and smoke detection. We map these requirements during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the scope and budget reflect compliance from the start.

faqs.q: Can I legally rent a casita behind a San Antonio house?
faqs.a: It depends on zoning, how the structure was built and whether it was permitted. San Antonio has rules for accessory dwelling units, and older casitas may or may not meet them. We review records and physical conditions and explain what would be required to bring the unit into compliance, including any electrical, plumbing or egress corrections, so you can factor the cost into your offer.

faqs.q: Do historic rules apply to a Monte Vista fourplex?
faqs.a: If the property is in the Monte Vista Historic District, exterior changes require review by the Office of Historic Preservation or the Historic and Design Review Commission. That includes windows, porches, stairs and additions. Interior work is generally not reviewed. We check status and plan exterior work to meet the guidelines, which often means repairing original features rather than replacing them.

faqs.q: How do you renovate a fourplex with tenants in place?
faqs.a: We renovate vacant units first, then complete occupied units as leases end or tenants move into finished units. Shared-system work is scheduled with written notice and short shutoffs. Our field manager coordinates access, keeps common areas safe and documents progress so you can keep tenants informed throughout the project. In converted houses where units share a single water heater or drain, we plan that work for one short window instead of several.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in San Antonio, TX | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor in San Antonio: pier leveling, rewiring, hail roofs and historic-district work bid for Limited or Standard loans.
fha-203k.intro: An FHA 203(k) loan can be the bridge between a San Antonio buyer and a house that needs real work, such as a Beacon Hill bungalow with sloping floors or a northeast ranch with a hail-worn roof and an outdated panel. The loan combines the purchase and repair costs into one mortgage, with repairs completed after closing through a controlled draw process. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and we work with buyers, agents, lenders and HUD consultants across San Antonio to prepare the detailed bids and draw schedules the program requires. We coordinate licensed local contractors, manage permits and, where needed, historic approvals, and keep everyone informed through each draw. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps buyers understand likely repair costs before writing an offer.

sections.h2: Choosing Limited or Standard in San Antonio
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to the program's $75,000 cap. In San Antonio, it suits houses with a stable foundation that need updates such as a roof replacement, HVAC system, electrical panel, water heater, windows, flooring, paint or a kitchen and bath refresh. Many brick ranches on the northeast and north-central sides fit this profile.

The Standard 203(k) is required when the project involves structural repairs, and in San Antonio that most often means foundation work. Leveling a pier-and-beam bungalow in Tobin Hill or Beacon Hill, replacing rotted floor framing on a Westside cottage, or rebuilding a failing addition puts the project in Standard territory. The Standard program has a $5,000 minimum repair requirement and requires a HUD consultant who inspects the property, prepares the work write-up and approves draws. We coordinate with the consultant so our bid matches the write-up and so the schedule sequences foundation work before interior finishes.

sections.h2: San Antonio houses that fit the program
sections.body:
The best 203(k) candidates in San Antonio are houses in good locations priced down by fixable problems. A 1920s bungalow in Beacon Hill or Alta Vista that needs leveling, rewiring, plumbing and a kitchen is a classic Standard project and can give a buyer access to a close-in neighborhood. A 1960s ranch near Fort Sam Houston with a tired roof, old HVAC and a dated kitchen is a typical Limited project.

There are local cautions. In historic districts, exterior repairs such as window replacement or porch rebuilding may require approval from the Office of Historic Preservation, which affects both the scope and the timeline. Unpermitted additions common on the Westside and South Side may need to be legalized or removed for the loan to close. Older homes require lead-safe work practices when paint is disturbed. We identify these issues early so buyers, agents and lenders can plan around them. VA buyers considering a renovation loan face similar questions, and the same early review helps them.

A 203(k) loan relies on detailed paperwork. The lender requires a contractor bid broken out by line item with labor and materials, matching the consultant's write-up on a Standard loan. Repair funds are released in draws as work is completed and inspected. Projects above the $15,000 threshold carry additional inspection and documentation requirements.

Genstone's estimators prepare bids in the format lenders and consultants expect, and our field manager coordinates draw inspections. We do not require upfront payment, and our draws are tied to completed work, which matches the way the program releases funds. Permits are pulled through the City of San Antonio Development Services Department, and historic approvals are requested early where needed. Many 203(k) buyers are paying rent while the work happens, so we order long-lead items like HVAC equipment and windows promptly after closing to keep the move-in date realistic. Each draw request goes out with photos and inspection sign-offs attached, so the consultant or lender can release funds without chasing paperwork.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover foundation leveling in San Antonio?
faqs.a: Yes, through the Standard 203(k). Foundation work is structural, so the Limited version does not apply. We coordinate with the HUD consultant, a licensed foundation contractor and, where needed, an engineer to scope, price and document the repair. Leveling is scheduled first so the new drywall, trim and tile are not cracked by later adjustments. Engineer letters and any foundation warranty are kept for the buyer's records.

faqs.q: Does a historic district complicate a 203(k)?
faqs.a: It adds a step. Exterior work in a local historic district may need approval from the Office of Historic Preservation or the Historic and Design Review Commission. That can affect which repairs are practical and how long the project takes. We check district status early, design the exterior scope to meet the guidelines and submit for approval promptly, so interior work can proceed while the application is reviewed.

faqs.q: Do you work with San Antonio agents and lenders?
faqs.a: Yes. Agents and loan officers often bring us in early to give buyers a realistic repair estimate before an offer is finalized. We then provide the detailed bid the loan requires, coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans and keep everyone updated as draws are requested, inspected and released. That shared document keeps the option period, appraisal and closing on track.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in San Antonio, TX | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: San Antonio REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: freeze-damaged crawlspaces, hail roofs, vandalism, historic districts and vacant-building rules.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in San Antonio
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned homes in San Antonio tend to arrive with a familiar list of problems: pier-and-beam houses with split pipes in the crawlspace after a freeze, ranches with hail-damaged roofs that have been leaking for months, stolen condensers and copper, and overgrown lots drawing code complaints. In historic districts, a vacant house can also draw attention from the Office of Historic Preservation if it deteriorates. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, which use us as a preferred contractor, to stabilize and renovate REO properties across San Antonio. Preservation, inspections and code compliance run through Genstone Field Services, and the renovation itself runs through our construction team. We coordinate licensed local contractors, document every condition and help move each asset toward the right disposition.

sections.h2: What San Antonio REO properties typically need
sections.body:
Freeze damage is a recurring issue in vacant San Antonio homes, especially older pier-and-beam houses on the Westside, South Side and East Side where supply lines run exposed under the floor. Winter Storm Uri in 2021 left many vacant properties with burst pipes that went unnoticed for weeks, and the resulting water damage spread into floors, walls and framing. Roof damage from hail and wind is also common, and leaks in a vacant house can lead to collapsed ceilings and mold.

Theft and vandalism are frequent, including stolen AC condensers, water heaters, appliances and copper wiring. On older homes, deferred maintenance shows up as rotted siding, failing porches and foundation settlement. Unpermitted additions may have deteriorated faster than the original house. Our initial inspection documents each condition with photos and a preliminary scope so servicers can decide between repair and as-is disposition quickly. On homes near creeks and drainage channels, we also note any signs of past flash flooding, since water lines on walls or silt in the crawlspace change both the scope and the disclosure picture.

REO projects in San Antonio usually follow three phases. Stabilization includes securing the property, winterizing plumbing, tarping roofs, removing debris and addressing hazards. In San Antonio that preservation work is usually performed by Genstone Field Services crews. Repairs focus on items that affect value or financing, such as roof replacement, plumbing and electrical repairs, foundation leveling and HVAC replacement. Listing preparation follows with paint, flooring, cleaning and curb appeal.

Our estimators can price multiple scope options, from minimal repairs for an as-is investor sale to a fuller renovation that meets FHA and VA minimum property requirements, which matters in a market with many military buyers. Debris removal is included in every estimate. Draws are tied to completed, documented work, and asset managers can follow progress through milestone reports.

The right scope often depends on where the house sits. A brick ranch near Randolph or Fort Sam Houston usually sells best after enough repair to qualify for VA or FHA financing, because that opens the property to the largest buyer pool. A small Westside cottage with a failing addition may net more as an as-is sale to an investor. Our estimates lay out both so the asset manager can compare.

sections.h2: Code, vacant-building rules and historic districts
sections.body:
San Antonio code enforcement responds to vacant-property issues such as overgrown yards, open structures, trash and unsafe conditions, and violations can lead to citations and liens. The city also operates a vacant building program that requires registration and maintenance standards for certain vacant properties, with particular attention to historic districts and the downtown area. Genstone Field Services monitors properties, keeps yards maintained and responds to notices promptly.

For properties in local historic districts, exterior repairs require approval from the Office of Historic Preservation, and demolition or neglect can draw scrutiny. We plan exterior work to meet the guidelines and request approvals early. Permits for repair work go through the City of San Antonio Development Services Department or the relevant suburban building department. Lien waivers and contractor compliance documentation are collected on every job and organized for audit, and inspection sign-offs are kept with the project file so the eventual buyer's agent can see exactly what was repaired and permitted.

faqs.q: Do you winterize vacant San Antonio homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services winterizes plumbing on vacant homes and can insulate exposed crawlspace lines on pier-and-beam houses. After a freeze, we inspect previously winterized homes and document their condition so servicers know whether repairs are needed. That matters in San Antonio because hard freezes are rare enough that many vacant houses are not prepared for them, and a split line under a pier-and-beam floor can run unnoticed for a long time.

faqs.q: Can you work on REO homes in historic districts?
faqs.a: Yes. We plan exterior repairs to meet Office of Historic Preservation guidelines and request approvals early, so the property can be stabilized and marketed without code or preservation issues. Typical items include repairing original wood windows and siding, rebuilding porches with matching materials and keeping the roofline and exterior character intact, which buyers in districts like Dignowity Hill and Government Hill tend to value.

faqs.q: Do you cover San Antonio suburbs?
faqs.a: Yes. We work across Bexar County and nearby cities including Converse, Live Oak, Universal City, Schertz and Leon Valley, with consistent documentation across every property. Each address gets its own field manager, and we confirm the right permitting office before work begins, since much of the newer housing sits in suburban cities or unincorporated Bexar County rather than inside San Antonio city limits.
